title_en: Homily on the Paralytic at the Pool
author: Cyril of Jerusalem
occasion: A homily on the Gospel account of the healing at the pool of Bethesda (John 5), exhorting the congregation to seek Christ as the true healer of soul and body.
argument: Cyril presents Jesus as the physician of souls and bodies who heals the paralytic at the pool not through water but through his word. He interprets the paralytic's bed as a figure of the cross and the Song of Songs as a sober, nuptial prophecy of Christ's passion. The healing becomes a lesson against unbelief and a call to repentance: those healed by Christ must sin no more. Cyril closes by urging his hearers to flee to Christ for every need and to glorify God through their deeds.

outline.move: Cyril introduces Jesus as the savior who heals wherever he appears and describes the pool of Bethesda with its five porticoes and the paralytic who had lain there thirty-eight years.
Cyril expounds Jesus' question 'Do you want to be healed?' as drawing out faith, and contrasts the paralytic's lack of human help with the presence of the God-man who is the true fountain of life.

Cyril interprets the paralytic's bed as a figure of the cross, using the Song of Songs to show that its nuptial language soberly prefigures Christ's passion, including the silver of Judas' betrayal, the purple robe, and the pavement of Gabbatha; he mentions Proverbs only as a pedagogical stepping-stone to understanding the Song.
Cyril recounts the healed man's reply to the Jews, praises Jesus' hiddenness after the healing, and applies the command 'Sin no more' to every hearer, urging mastery over the flesh.
Cyril exhorts the congregation to flee to Christ in every need and concludes with a doxology.
Continuation of the closing exhortation and doxology; these are editorial subdivisions of the same closing material found in u02-open.

cast.name: Jesus
cast.who: The savior and chief physician who heals the paralytic by his word.

cast.name: The paralytic
cast.who: The man healed after thirty-eight years at the pool of Bethesda.

cast.name: The Jews
cast.who: Those who object to the healing on the Sabbath and refuse to believe.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle who walked on the water toward Jesus.

cast.name: Judas
cast.who: The betrayer whose silver began the passion.

cast.name: Pilate
cast.who: The governor in whose court was the pavement called Gabbatha.

cast.name: Simon the leper
cast.who: The host in whose house a woman poured ointment on Jesus' head.

voices.speaker: Jesus
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as 'he said' or quoted directly after narrative introductions.

voices.speaker: The paralytic (biblical reply)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'he says to him' or 'he replied'; his actual words from John 5 are quoted.

voices.speaker: The healed man (Cyril's rhetorical expansion)
voices.how_marked: Cyril composes an extended first-person speech for the healed man defending himself before the Jews; this is not a biblical quotation but Cyril's invention.

voices.speaker: The Jews
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'they said' or 'they were saying'.

key_terms.sense: Chief physician, a title for Christ as the healer of souls and bodies.
The pool of Bethesda where the sick awaited the stirring of the water.
The paralytic's bed or mat, which Jesus commands him to carry.
A litter or carrying frame, interpreted by Cyril as a figure of the cross.
Fountain or spring, used of Christ as the source of living water and life.
Salvation or healing, often both physical and spiritual in this homily.
Unbelief, especially the Jews' refusal to accept Jesus despite his works.
The Sabbath, on which Jesus heals and the Jews object.
Jesus' command to the healed man, applied by Cyril to all hearers as a call to repentance.
Flesh, understood by Cyril as the sphere of sinful passions rather than the physical body itself.
The stone pavement, identified with Gabbatha in Pilate's court, seen as a figure of the passion.

scripture: Cyril uses the Septuagint (LXX) text and its book names and Psalm numbering. Citations should be given in modern form with LXX Psalm numbering noted where it differs from the Hebrew (e.g., LXX Psalm 2 = Hebrew Psalm 2; LXX Psalm 50 = Hebrew Psalm 51).
uncertain: The precise liturgical occasion of the homily is not stated in the text.
The exact date of composition is uncertain; c. 350 is an approximation based on Cyril's episcopate.

_unresolved_facts.fix: Remove Pilate from cast. The text mentions 'ἐν τοῖς Πιλάτου' (in Pilate's [praetorium]) but does not name Pilate as a character; only his location is referenced.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Simon the leper, source_forms: ["Σίμων ὁ λεπρός"]
_unresolved_facts.fix: Remove Simon the leper from cast. The text mentions 'Σίμωνος τοῦ λεπροῦ' only as the owner of the house where the ointment was poured; he is not a speaking character or active figure in the homily.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The healed man (Cyril's rhetorical expansion), sections: ["u01-rem-close"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἴστε μου, φησί, πάντες τὴν πολυχρόνιον νόσον... ὁ ποιήσας με ὑγιῆ ἐκεῖνός μοι εἶπεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief should note that Cyril presents this as the healed man's actual reply to the Jews (introduced by 'φησί'), not clearly marked as Cyril's own rhetorical invention. The text presents it as the man's direct speech.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-mid move: 'mentions Proverbs only as a pedagogical stepping-stone to understanding the Song'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ εἰ μὴ νοεῖς τὰ ᾄσματα, ἐλθὲ ἐπὶ τὰς παροιμίας, καὶ ὁδῷ καὶ βαθμίσιν ἀνάβηθι ἐπ' ἐκεῖνα
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cyril mentions Proverbs (παροιμίας) as a stepping-stone, but the section also contains substantial interpretation of Proverbs itself ('ἡ σοφία ᾠκοδόμησεν ἑαυτῇ οἶκον', 'ἐράσθητι αὐτῆς καὶ τηρήσει σε') before returning to the Song of Songs, not merely a passing mention.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u02-rem-early, u02-rem-mid, u02-rem-close move: 'editorial subdivisions of the same closing material found in u02-open'
_unresolved_facts.fix: These sections contain material that is NOT in u02-open. u02-open begins mid-sentence with 'καὶ εἰ νοσοῦμεν...' and ends with the doxology. u02-rem-early repeats the exhortation material, u02-rem-mid contains the transitional sentence about the sermon extending too long, and u02-rem-close contains the doxology. They are not subdivisions of u02-open but overlapping/parallel material in a different textual arrangement.
